section_title: What can a church with little strength expect from Christ?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 To the angel of the church in Philadelphia write: These are the words of the One who is holy and true, who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open. 8 I know your deeds. Behold, I have placed before you an open door, which no one can shut. I know that you have only a little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name.

9 As for those who belong to the synagogue of Satan, who claim to be Jews but are liars instead, I will make them come and bow down at your feet, and they will know that I love you. 10 Because you have kept My command to persevere, I will also keep you from the hour of testing that is about to come upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth. 11 I am coming soon. Hold fast to what you have, so that no one will take your crown.

12 The one who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it. Upon him I will write the name of My God, and the name of the city of My God (the new Jerusalem that comes down out of heaven from My God), and My new name. 13 He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.

context_lines: Philadelphia receives encouragement from the One who is holy and true and holds the key of David. The language recalls [Isaiah 22:20–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/22.htm), where Eliakim receives authority over David’s house. Here Jesus has authority that no opponent can overturn: what He opens stays open, and what He shuts stays shut.

The church has little strength, yet has kept His word and remained loyal to His name. Its limited strength does not prevent Him from placing an open door before it. He promises that the opponents described in verse 9 will come to recognize His love for this community. The accusation concerns those opponents, without making every Jewish person its target.

Jesus also promises protection from an approaching hour of testing and calls the church to hold fast so no one takes its crown. The promise encourages continued faithfulness. It does not make the need to persevere disappear.

The final images emphasize belonging and permanence: a pillar that remains in God’s temple, God’s name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Christ’s new name. The church’s future rests on the authority and love of the One addressing it.
common_interpretation_lines: The open door is commonly connected with access granted by Christ. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) includes both entrance into the Lord’s joy and opportunity for faithful work. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/3.htm) emphasizes opportunity to proclaim the gospel. The image can carry more than one closely related application without reducing Christ’s authority to a technique for getting the results someone wants.

The hour of testing receives substantially different explanations. Wesley connects it with persecution under Trajan within the Roman Empire. Gill places it in a later conflict affecting the churches and describes Christ preserving His people amid the distress. [John Walvoord’s own commentary](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_03.htm), representing a reading in which Christ gathers the church before a future worldwide tribulation, understands it as deliverance from that period. This is a real difference over the setting and manner of protection, not a teaching on which every church agrees.

The Greek verb tereo means to guard or keep. [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/5083.htm) places this promise alongside [John 17:15](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/17.htm), where Jesus asks that His people be kept from evil while remaining in the world. The word supports the promise of protection; deciding exactly how that protection happens requires the passage’s wider context. A word definition alone does not establish an entire end-times timetable.
god_plan_lines: The key from David’s house in Isaiah becomes part of the picture of Christ’s authority over His people. The destination named in the promise is the new Jerusalem. In [Revelation 21:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/21.htm), that city descends from God, and God dwells with His people as death and mourning pass away.

The pillar and written names express a lasting place with God. Revelation later says that God and the Lamb themselves are the city’s temple; see [21:22–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/revelation/21.htm). These pictures carry the hope beyond a fragile community’s present security to life permanently shared with Him. They do not require us to settle every disputed detail about the intervening trial.
